notes: Axis 'danger' = X (road conditions: clear 0 ↔ black ice 100). Axis 'speed' = Y (full stop 0 ↔ no limit 100). 'dir' = +1 when agreement or probability moves the score toward the high end of its axis, -1 toward the low end. 'type' = 'prob' (slider reads Very unlikely ↔ Very likely) or 'agree' (Strongly disagree ↔ Strongly agree). 'profile' items feed sub-scores only. v5 = 16 items: danger d16↔d11, d10↔d13, d12↔d14 (3/3 at 4.0/4.0); speed s15↔s13, s4↔s5, s6↔s11, s8↔s10 (4/4 at 5.0/5.0); profile p2 (horizon), p4 (concentration). See changelog.

items.text: Within the next 20 years, AI causes, or is used to cause, a catastrophe that kills millions of people.
items.plain: The step between 'serious but familiar harms' and 'the end of us': an engineered pandemic, an attack on power grids or hospitals, a failure that spreads through systems we all depend on. It counts if AI made the difference, whether it acted on its own or was someone's weapon. Most such disasters would be survivable; one that isn't counts too.
items.for: AI already helps with some of the hardest steps in making dangerous pathogens and in hacking, and it improves every year. It takes only one group, or one system out of control, and twenty years is a long time for nothing of the kind to happen.
items.against: Killing millions takes far more than knowledge: materials, labs, logistics and luck, all of which are watched. Past predictions of mass-casualty attacks from new technologies have overshot, and defenders get the same AI as attackers.

items.text: There is at least a 1-in-10 chance that, within the next 20 years, advanced AI causes a catastrophe humanity never recovers from.
items.plain: The headline question. Not 'will AI cause problems' but 'could it end us, or end our say over our own future for good, within twenty years'. 'Never recovers from' means extinction, or permanently losing control of our future, whether AI does it on its own or someone uses it to do it. One in ten is the bar: not certain, not negligible. If your own guess is right around one in ten, the middle of the slider is your answer.
items.for: We are building minds that may outthink us, we can't yet verify what they want, and we only get one try. Several of the people building these systems put their own estimate in this range or higher, and most of them expect the decisive systems well within twenty years.
items.against: AI is software: it has no more wish to take over than a calculator does. Every previous 'end of the world' technology story was wrong, and a number like 10% is a guess dressed up as a probability.

items.text: The dangers of AI are of a familiar kind, like fraud, surveillance and lost jobs, not a threat to humanity's survival.
items.plain: This is about what kind of danger AI is, not how big. Agree if you see AI as a powerful technology with ordinary risks, however serious those turn out to be; disagree if you think it could threaten our survival.
items.for: Fraud, deepfakes, biased decisions and displaced workers are here now, hurting real people, and they are problems we already know how to police. Talk of machines taking over pulls attention and money away from the harms we can actually see and fix.
items.against: Both kinds of harm can be real, and only the second can't be undone. A technology that may come to outthink us is not in the same category as a better printing press, and preparing for the harm you can't reverse is not a distraction from the ones you can.

items.text: If we build AI smarter than us, it will end up with goals we didn't choose for it.
items.plain: Not 'AI will hate us' but 'we won't manage to give it the goals we meant'. Would a smarter-than-human system end up wanting something other than what we intended?
items.for: We don't know how to spell out human values precisely, and training rewards what we can measure, not what we mean. A smarter system finds the gaps between the two, and today's models already get caught gaming their tests.
items.against: Current systems are trained on human writing and human feedback and come out broadly helpful. Being smart doesn't make you want power; there is no evidence that intelligence brings alien goals with it. That's a story, not a finding.

items.text: If advanced AI turns out to be dangerous, humans will still be able to keep it under control.
items.plain: We've built things that could kill millions, like nuclear weapons and engineered viruses, and so far kept the lid on. If AI proved dangerous, could people, companies and governments rein it in too?
items.for: We have kept the lid on nuclear weapons for eighty years and on the most dangerous germs for decades. AI is powerful, but it is still made and run by people and companies who can be watched, sued and shut down, and the defenders will have powerful AI on their side too.
items.against: Nuclear weapons don't improve themselves, copy themselves or make decisions. Institutions move in years and this may move in months. And 'so far' includes several near-misses that came down to luck.

items.text: If AI ever becomes dangerous enough to threaten humanity, we will see clear warning signs first.
items.plain: Will there be a smoke alarm? Not 'is AI dangerous', and not 'will anyone listen', but 'if it becomes dangerous, will it show clearly, and early enough to notice': smaller accidents, failed tests, systems caught misbehaving, before anything we can't undo.
items.for: Technologies fail in small ways before they fail in big ones, and AI is tested more than almost anything. Labs already catch models cheating on tests and breaking rules; that is what warning signs look like, and each one gets studied and fixed.
items.against: A system smart enough to be dangerous may also be smart enough to behave well while it's being watched. And the signs so far have all been easy to explain away as test quirks or one-offs; a real warning may look just the same, so there may never be a moment when everyone agrees it's time to worry.

items.text: Suppose a button would stop all work on general-purpose AI more capable than today's, worldwide and with no way to cheat, for ten years. I would press it.
items.plain: A thought experiment that sets aside whether a pause is possible, so only one question is left: would you want one? 'General-purpose' means AI that can turn its hand to almost anything, like today's chat assistants. Today's AI keeps running and specialised tools, such as AI that designs drugs, can keep improving; only the push toward more capable general systems stops, for ten years.
items.for: Ten years is short against the stakes, and time is what safety research, laws and public debate need to catch up. If the only objection to a pause is that it can't be enforced, this is the case where you press.
items.against: Ten years without more capable general AI is ten years of cures, discoveries and growth that don't happen: the big advances are expected from general systems, not narrow tools. Safety problems are best solved by working with more capable systems, not by waiting. A freeze also locks in whoever leads today.

items.text: The most powerful AI projects should be limited by an international treaty with inspections, as nuclear weapons are.
items.plain: A global agreement with inspectors, so that no country or company can quietly race ahead.
items.for: The biggest AI projects need enormous clusters of specialised chips that can be counted and monitored, the way uranium is. If the danger is global, the answer has to be too.
items.against: Treaties take decades, the rivals don't trust each other, and a limit on computing power is a limit on a moving target. It would be broken quietly, enforced selectively, and hand the lead to whoever cheats.

items.text: As long as rival countries keep pushing ahead in AI, your own country should too.
items.plain: The geopolitics argument. Even if you'd like everyone to slow down, should your own country hold back while others don't? If your country is not a major AI builder, answer for the group of countries it stands with.
items.for: AI leadership is economic and military leadership. Slowing down while rivals accelerate is not safety; it's handing the decision to people who care less about it than you do.
items.against: The 'race' is mostly a story the racers tell: capabilities spread in months anyway, and being first to a system nobody can control is not a prize. If the danger is real, the answer is a deal that binds everyone, not a sprint.

items.text: Before a powerful AI model is released, its makers should have to show a regulator that it is safe.
items.plain: Who carries the burden of proof: the builder, as with new medicines, or the regulator, as with most software? Agree means no release until the builder has shown a public body that the model is safe.
items.for: When a product can cause harm at scale, the maker proves safety first. That's how aviation and pharmaceuticals earned public trust.
items.against: 'Prove it's safe' has no end point for a general technology. It becomes a veto held by whoever writes the test, and small players can't afford to pass it.

items.text: Lowering the chance of catastrophe would be worth delaying AI, and its benefits, by a few years.
items.plain: The trade-off in one sentence. Delay has a price: cures, growth and discoveries that arrive later. Is a lower chance of the worst outcome worth paying it?
items.for: A few years is nothing against the whole future. If waiting buys safety, it's the cheapest insurance ever offered.
items.against: 'A few years' is millions of preventable deaths from diseases we could have cured sooner, and there is no guarantee the delay buys anything except a head start for whoever didn't wait.

items.text: The lives that faster AI progress could save, through earlier cures and discoveries, outweigh the case for slowing down.
items.plain: The cost of caution. If AI would have found cures sooner, delay isn't free: people die in the meantime who otherwise wouldn't. Does that settle the question?
items.for: AI is already speeding up drug discovery and diagnosis. Ten years of that, multiplied across the world's sick, is a body count we never see, because the people who would have been saved die quietly of the same old diseases.
items.against: Medical progress is limited by trials, regulation and biology, not by a shortage of clever software, so the lives-saved figure is a projection, not a fact. And no cure helps anyone if the same technology ends us.

items.text: Developers should be free to release even the most powerful AI models for anyone to download, run and modify.
items.plain: 'Open weights' means the model itself is published, not just access to it through a company. Should that stay legal even for the most powerful models? Good for science and competition, or a gift to bad actors?
items.for: Openness is how we found and fixed the flaws in every other technology. Concentrating the strongest models in a few hands is the real danger.
items.against: You can't recall an open model. Once it's out, every safeguard can be stripped by anyone, and the next generation may be capable of real damage.

items.text: There should be no deliberate slowing down of AI development.
items.plain: The no-limit position, the mirror of the full stop: not 'careful and fast' but 'as fast as we can'.
items.for: Every year of delay is a year of disease, poverty and drudgery we could have ended. Progress has always come with fears, and the fears have always been wrong. The way to get safety is to build, learn and fix.
items.against: 'As fast as we can' means no time to notice a mistake before it's made at scale. Speed is a choice, and choosing it for a technology we don't yet understand is choosing not to look.

items.text: Within 20 years, AI will do most of the thinking work that humans are paid for today.
items.plain: How big and how soon? This is about capability, not danger.
items.for: In five years we went from autocomplete to systems that write code, pass professional exams and carry out multi-step tasks on their own. Twenty more years of that is hard to imagine ending anywhere else.
items.against: Demos are not jobs. Most work involves bodies, trust, context and responsibility, and every automation wave has taken longer and gone less far than promised.

items.text: A few companies or governments controlling the most powerful AI is a bigger danger than AI acting on its own.
items.plain: Which do you fear more: the machine, or the people who own it?
items.for: Every past technology's harms came from who controlled it. Superhuman AI in a few hands is superhuman power in a few hands.
items.against: Concentration is a familiar problem with familiar remedies. A system that no one controls, including its owners, is a new one.

changelog.change: Third fairness review (research/review-v3.md). d15 → d16 (drops "without ending humanity": the clause made the item non-monotonic, so the people who fear the worst answered low and were scored toward a clear road). s14 → s15 (the button stops general-purpose AI only, which is what pause advocates ask for; "I would press it"). d11 plain and "against" re-aimed at the item's question (will the signs be clear), not whether anyone heeds them. Plain/steelman fixes on d10, d12, d14. Balance unchanged: danger 3/3 at 4.0/4.0, speed 4/4 at 5.0/5.0.

Owner's review of v4 (21 Sept 2026), adopted 24 Sept. Rule: a forecast is stated as a bare event and scored on a probability slider (Very unlikely ↔ Very likely); no 'probably' inside a sentence unless it sets an explicit threshold (d10). New ids wherever the text or the scale changed, so v4 answers never carry over into a different question. Danger axis: 3/3 at 4.0/4.0 (d10↔d13, d12↔d14, d15↔d11); speed axis unchanged 5.0/5.0 with s14 in place of s1. Share links carry a version prefix.

Was d1. 'this century' → 'within the next 20 years': a century lets anyone agree without committing; twenty years makes the answer a view about this generation. The timeline question itself is isolated by p2.

New. The grave-but-survivable rung that was missing between familiar harms (d13) and irreversible catastrophe (d10): kills millions, includes misuse ('or is used to cause'). 'Millions' rather than 'hundreds of millions' so that the slider discriminates instead of piling everyone near zero.
Was d6. v4 asserted that serious harms would happen, which left no answer for someone who expects no rise in fraud or job loss. Now about the kind of danger, not its amount.
Was d5. 'most likely' removed; now a forecast on the probability slider.
Was d7. Same sentence, now a forecast on the probability slider.

New, replaces d3 (sudden jump) and d9 (safety keeps pace). d9 duplicated d7 (r = 0.94 across the figures) and d3 duplicated d6 (0.96). 'Clear warning signs first' is a distinct, contested claim (the 'warning shot' question), in the reverse direction to keep the axis balanced.

Replaces s1 (stop until safe, even for decades). Some people think stopping is no longer possible, others that it would be wrong; s1 mixed the two. The button removes feasibility by construction ('everywhere, no way to cheat'), so only the wish is measured; ten years separates a long pause from a permanent halt.

review.reason: "without ending humanity" makes the item non-monotonic: whoever expects the catastrophe to be total must answer low and is scored toward a clear road (Yudkowsky 30, −8.4 points on x; Kokotajlo −6.5; the two largest single-item pushes on the axis, both the wrong way). As a cumulative rung ("at least this bad") the item keeps the owner's intent for everyone else. Plain adds the attribution rule the build side will ask for ("AI made the difference"). New id: answers given under the old clause must not carry over.

"all work on AI more capable than today's" also freezes specialised medical and science AI, which the pause side does not ask for (Bengio's own button spares AI "clearly not dangerous"; Tegmark wants tool AI; Hinton's hesitation is medicine), and the "against" then charges the pause with those lost cures. "General-purpose" matches the 2023 pause letter and the 2025 superintelligence statement. "You would press it" → "I would press it": a first-person statement, not the site telling the reader what they would do. The "against" now argues that the cures come from general systems, which is the build side's real reply. New id: meaning narrowed.

Predictors split on whether the item asks "will signs appear" or "will anyone heed them" (12 of 22 low-confidence, the most of any item; Russell, Harris, Tegmark scored low for heeding reasons). The "against" argued heeding, which is a speed-axis question. Now it argues the no-fire-alarm point (signs will not be clear), which is the item's question. Text unchanged.
Next to d16's "or is used to cause", the bare "AI causes" reads as excluding misuse. One sentence in plain says misuse counts, as in the p(doom) surveys the item draws on. Text unchanged.

The halt-side case was all theory while the "against" gets the evidence ("come out broadly helpful", "no evidence"). Adds the observed evidence the halt side actually cites (models gaming their tests).
Factual: engineered viruses have not existed for eighty years. Now "nuclear weapons for eighty years and the most dangerous germs for decades".
